entry.title: Legacy Excel to XML Conversion in Integration Suite: Handling BIFF5/Excel 5.0 during PI/PO migration
entry.content:
Migrating from PI/PO to Integration Suite comes with unexpected challenges - like handling legacy Excel files from the 90s. In this first post of our migration series, I'll show you how to convert those old BIFF5/Excel 5.0 files to XML when standard approaches fail. 

The Challenge

While excellent resources exist on Excel-to-XML conversion in CPI (see posts by @engswee, @yusufbayasal, and @RoohiJain), they assume modern Excel formats (BIFF8/XLSX). The Excel files we needed to convert were too old for these standard approaches, failing with the error:  "The supplied spreadsheet seems to be Excel 5.0/7.0 (BIFF5) format. POI only supports BIFF8 format (from Excel versions 97/2000/XP/2003)": 

javax.script.ScriptException: java.lang.Exception: 
org.apache.poi.hssf.OldExcelFormatException: 
The supplied spreadsheet seems to be Excel 5.0/7.0 (BIFF5) format. 
POI only supports BIFF8 format (from Excel versions 97/2000/XP/2003)

This error tells us something important: our Excel file is in the older BIFF5 format (used by Excel 5.0/7.0/95), which Apache POI's standard `HSSFWorkbook` and `XSSFWorkbook` classes cannot read. 

The solution

Apache POI provides a specialized utility class called OldExcelExtractor designed specifically for extracting text from these legacy Excel formats.

Preparation

Download poi jar file and imported into our CPI iFlow. To download it, go to the download page of Apache POI https://poi.apache.org/download.html >> Find the latest stable release >> select Binary Artifacts (https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/apache/poi/poi/5.5.1) >> select poi.x.x.x.jar. 

Upload it to the iFlow under References >> Add >> Archive, select the jar file and add. 

Implementation

We implmented the conversion in two steps: 

  • convert the Excel file into CSV format
  • convert CSV format into XML

Of couse one can combine both steps into the groovy script. But we did so to reduce custom scripting to minimum. 

Convert Excel to CSV

The script below has a hard-coded assumption about column count (every 10th row). Please adjust it to suite your needs. 

import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message;
import org.apache.poi.hssf.extractor.OldExcelExtractor;

def Message processData(Message message) {
    byte[] bodyByteArray = message.getBody(java.io.InputStream).bytes
    OldExcelExtractor extractor = new OldExcelExtractor(new ByteArrayInputStream(bodyByteArray))
    String extractedText = extractor.getText()
    extractor.close()
    
    // Split into rows (OldExcelExtractor uses \n as row separator)
    def rows = extractedText.split('\n')
    def cvsData = ""
    
	//Convert tab-separated rows to pipe-separated format
	//Note: the legacy excel file has exactly 10 columns per row
    for(int i=1; i<rows.length; i++) {
        if (i % 10 == 0) {
            cvsData += rows[i] + '\n'
        } else {
            cvsData += rows[i] + '|'
        }
    }
    
    message.setBody(cvsData) 
    return message;
}

Convert CSV into XML

Here we used the XSD schema exported from PI/PO, and converting into XML skipping the first line. 

That's it. Old Excel formats shouldn't slow down your PI/PO migration. With Apache POI's `OldExcelExtractor` and the approach outlined above, you can automate the conversion of even the oldest Excel files - no manual intervention required.

Coming up next in this series: More real-world migration challenges and the exact solutions we used to solve them. Have you encountered legacy format issues in your migration? Drop a comment below!

entry.title: Mapping SAP Process Orchestration JMS (IBM MQ) Adapter to SAP Integration Suite IBM MQ Adapter
entry.content:
This blog post is part of the series Master Blog: SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite Migration – Tool and Guidance exploring how to migrate various integration patterns from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite using the Migration Tool.

Objective of this Blog

In this blog, we will focus on the mapping of SAP Process Orchestration JMS (IBM MQ) adapter — with Transport Protocol “WebSphereMQ (MQSeries) JMS Provider” and Message Protocol both “JMS 1.x” or “JMS 2.0”) — to SAP Integration Suite IBM MQ adapter.

Since the Migration Tool skips the SAP Process Orchestration JMS (IBM MQ) adapter, the approach described in this blog will help to manually configure both Sender and Receiver IBM MQ adapters in SAP Integration Suite iFlows based on source JMS (IBM MQ) SAP Process Orchestration scenarios.

Related Blogs 

  • IBM MQ JMS Adapter for SAP Integration Suite
  • Integrating IBM MQ On-Premise with SAP Cloud Integration Using the IBM MQ Adapter

SAP Process Orchestration JMS Adapter Modules

In SAP Process Orchestration, the following JMS Adapter Modules are commonly used to convert message payloads between binary and XML formats:                       

  • SAP XI JMS Adapter/ConvertJMSMessageToBinary
  • SAP XI JMS Adapter/ConvertBinaryToXMBMessage
  • SAP XI JMS Adapter/ConvertMessageToBinary
  • SAP XI JMS Adapter/SendBinarytoXIJMSService

In SAP Process Orchestration, these modules are often required when integrating with JMS providers such as IBM MQ. However, in SAP Integration Suite they are not required, as their functionality is provided directly by the IBM MQ adapter itself. The IBM MQ adapter in SAP Integration Suite offers built-in options for message conversion, allowing users to select either byte or text message formats directly in the adapter configuration.

Variants

Based on the SAP Process Orchestration source parameters, the migration will result in three different target variants:

- Sender

  • JMS Poll
  • JMS Subscribe

- Receiver:

  • JMS

Sender

The source Sender JMS MQ channel must have the following properties:

  • Adapter Type: JMS
  • Sender
  • Transport Protocol: WebSphereMQ (MQSeries) JMS Provider
  • Message protocol: JMS 1.x or JMS 2.0

The relevant Sender variants — JMS Poll and JMS Subscribe — are detailed below (REST variant doesn’t apply).

JMS Poll

JMS Poll implements a message retrieval mechanism where the IBM MQ JMS Sender Adapter actively polls messages from IBM MQ queues or topics at defined intervals, using a request-based approach to check for new messages periodically.

** In addition, some functionalities — such as correlation ID mapping — cannot be mapped directly but can be configured in the SAP Integration Suite IBM MQ adapter. E.g., in the receiver adapter, it can be set dynamically using an exchange header or property.

entry.title: SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite Migration - Alert Rules via SAP Cloud ALM
entry.content:
SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite Migration – Alert Rules via SAP Cloud ALM

Objective

The goal of this blog is to explain how to migrate your alert rules from SAP Process Orchestration and set up proactive monitoring for SAP Integration Suite exclusively using SAP Cloud ALM. We will cover the end-to-end setup including:

  • SAP BTP Cockpit configuration and endpoint creation.
  • Service and Endpoint configuration within SAP Cloud ALM.
  • Setting up alerts, filters, and event actions in Integration & Exception Monitoring.

SAP PO Alerts
In SAP Process Orchestration, you are likely used to creating Alert Rules in the NetWeaver Administrator (NWA) or Integration Directory. This is where you managed your active rules and their consumers (like ALERT-TO-MAIL).

As you can see below in the Message Header Rules tab, we would specifically filter our alerts using Integration Directory objects, such as the Service Interface, Communication Component, or the full Integrated Configuration (ICO):

Understanding the Transition to SAP Cloud ALM

When migrating your integration scenarios from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite, recreating your alerting mechanisms is a critical step. By using SAP Cloud ALM for your monitoring, you establish a connection point that improves visibility for all connected systems and ensures that integration errors are automatically detected and communicated.

Step 1: SAP BTP Cockpit Configuration

To connect SAP Cloud ALM with SAP Integration Suite, you must first create an endpoint in the SAP BTP Cockpit capable of retrieving Message Logs and Artifact Health data.

  • Navigate to your Subaccount from the Global Account in SAP BTP Cockpit.
  • Go to Services -> Instances and Subscriptions and choose Create.
  • Select the Process Integration Runtime Service and choose the integration-flow plan.

  • Add the following roles to the instance: MonitoringDataRead and MonitoringArtifactsDeploy.

  • After creating the instance, open it to create a Service Key.
  • Provide a descriptive name, set the Key Type to Client ID/Secret, and save the key in JSON format securely, as it will be required in later steps.

Step 2: SAP Cloud ALM Configuration

With the BTP endpoint prepared, the next phase is establishing the connection in SAP Cloud ALM. The user performing this needs specific roles: x_landscape_Administrator and x_landscape_SecurityAdministrator.

  • Access Administration and navigate to Landscape Management.

  • Under Services & Systems, you can attempt to automatically import your service by navigating to Configuration -> Import of Subscribed SAP Services.

  • If an automatic import isn't possible (which typically happens if the daily synchronization job hasn't run yet, the service is registered under a different customer number, or local access controls restrict your visibility), you can manually add a New Service. To do this, define parameters such as the Name and the System Number. To find your System Number, log into SAP for Me, navigate to 'Portfolio & Products' > 'My Product Portfolio', click on your specific product, and look under the 'Systems' tab for the tenant's unique identifier. Finally, select the Service Type (SAP Integration Suite) and input the Root URL / Logon URL that you copied from your saved Service Key.

  • Once the service is created, select Add in the Endpoints section and paste the Service Key details you saved earlier to automatically fill the parameters, then click Check Connection.

Step 3: Setting Up Alerts and Notifications

Now that the external systems are connected, you can configure the actual alert rules using the Integration & Exception Monitoring section in Operations.

To perform this, users need roles such as ops_im_IntegrationArchitect, ops_im_IntegrationOwner, or x_calm_GlobalAdministrator.

  • Select your newly configured service from the Managed Components list (under Services) and click Apply.

  • Access Edit Configuration for the service and turn on Data Collection to begin gathering monitoring data

 

  • Navigate to Events to add the specific events used for alerts.

  • For individual Integration Flow exceptions, add an event and set the Event Name to "Erroneous CPI Message Detected (Single)". To monitor specific messages or restrict events to certain integration flows, you can create custom filters. In the Filters tab, you can define filter parameters for specific integration flows. For example, you can limit the alert to a single interface by specifying its Artifact Name or Artifact ID, or include multiple interfaces by providing a list of names. Furthermore, you can use powerful combinations by pairing the Artifact Name with specific Statuses or Error Messages (e.g., only triggering the alert if 'iFlow_A' fails with an HTTP 500 error).  For those of used to SAP PO, think of the Artifact Name filter as the direct replacement for the Service Interface or ICO filters we saw in the Message Header Rules at the beginning of this post.

  • You can define specific parameters (like triggering the event for errors older than 5 minutes) and use the Filters tab to restrict the events to specific integration flows.

Post-Configuration Activities: Event Actions and Customizing Output

Just like manual fine-tuning steps in a interface migration, your event routing will need a few final touches:

 

  • Select verified recipients from the Recipient section. If your recipients aren't listed, add them by going to SAP Cloud ALM > Operations > Notification Management, clicking the '+' icon, and entering the target email addresses separated by commas.

 

  • When an error matches your defined parameters and filters, the system will automatically trigger an email notification containing key details like the integration artifact, message ID, status, and timestamp.

  • For single erroneous messages, you can highly customize the information displayed in the email up to 7 fields by choosing the appropriate attributes on the Grouping tab during Event configuration.

Conclusion

Migrating your alert rules to SAP Cloud ALM simplifies the monitoring process while guaranteeing that your SAP Integration Suite landscape remains highly visible. By establishing a secure BTP endpoint and defining granular event filters and notification actions, you can ensure reliable, scalable, and proactive error handling for all your newly migrated integration interfaces.

For additional questions related to the SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite migration, see FAQ – Migration from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite.

entry.title: Cloud Integration Pipeline - Datastore Extension UI
entry.content:
⚠️  Disclaimer: The UI described in this blog post is not an official product by SAP. If you are interested in using the UI, you can find the published code and set up instructions on the SAP-samples GitHub here: https://github.com/SAP-samples/cloud-integration-pipeline-datastore-extension-ui

 

Purpose and background

The pipeline in Cloud Integration is a well-established framework for asynchronous integrations. A blog post to explain the starting points for the pipeline can be found here.

In addition to the pipeline, we offer the datastore extension, which simplifies error handling via automatic retry jobs and APIs for resending and cancelling messages. For details on the datastore extension, please refer to this blog post. The datastore extension package provides automatic restart capabilities with Restart Jobs that are based on pre-delivered IFlows. In addition, it provides on-demand operations that require the use of API client tools such as Postman or Bruno. This is technical and error-prone to handle from a user perspective.

The UI introduced in this blog post is designed to provide a simplified and user-friendly approach to access these on-demand APIs.

On a technical level, it is relevant to note that the UI does not call Cloud Integration APIs directly. It calls IFlows of the Datastore Extension package, which are on-demand API Operations (Manage Retries and Manage Datastore Entries). It triggers a corresponding IFlow and operation and then displays the response.

This blog article introduces and explains the functionality of the Cloud Integration Pipeline Datastore Extension UI.

 

Overview of key features

The current version of the UI provides these capabilities, which are shown again in more detail in the “How to use the UI” section.

  • Visual overview of all available datastores relevant for the pipeline reprocessing, their messages and overdue messages
  • Search and filter capabilities to quickly locate specific datastores
  • Visual overview of all messages in each datastore
  • Search and filter capabilities to quickly locate specific messages
  • Action to restart messages from the UI
  • Action to move messages to another datastore or a no-retry datastore when located in a retry datastore
  • Action to delete/cancel messages 
  • Detailed view of message content (error, headers, payload)
  • Possibility to perform batch actions to restart, move, cancel several messages at once

 

How to use the UI

Datastore overview

The first screen of the UI shows a table with all the datastores, the number of messages, and the number of overdue messages. You can also search and filter the table for specific information. 

Datastore detail view and overview of messages

The second screen shows details of the selected datastore and contains a table with all the messages. 

One or more messages can be selected in the table and moved to another datastore or to a no-retry datastore. The messages can also be restarted or deleted from here.  

There are sorting capabilities available for the datastore entries table. They can be found behind the gear icon ⚙️. For example, the table can be sorted by the number of restarts and the timestamp of error, ascending or descending. 

There is also a filter hidden behind the same gear icon ⚙️.

Message detail view

When clicking on one of the rows in the datastore entries table the user is directed to a third screen with details about the error, headers and payload. If, after inspecting, the user decided what to do with the message it is also possible to perform the same move, delete and restart actions from this screen with the buttons in the top right corner.

 

Outlook & how to implement the UI

This project is available as an open-source project on the SAP-samples GitHub organization: https://github.com/SAP-samples/cloud-integration-pipeline-datastore-extension-ui . Here you can find the repository and a detailed implementation guide. If you notice any issues or have further ideas feel free to contribute to the project. You can also reach out to @lisarizzo or @mike_sibler  if you have any further questions.

entry.title: File Not Received in SAP PO After Server Change – Sender Channel Conflict Issue
entry.content:
Scenario Overview:

In our integration landscape, the data flow is:

AccordFT (MFT) → FTP → SAP PO → File (Archival) → SAP PO → SAP CAR/POSDTA

We are using a single standard interface and mapping for all countries. File processing is dynamic, and files are handled based on the country code.The MFT team confirmed that SAF files were successfully processed and sent from their end. However, SAP PO did not receive the files for one specific country, and the data was not delivered to the SAP CAR system.

Issue:

  • Files were successfully sent from MFT
  • No messages were visible in SAP PO for one country
  • Other country files were processed successfully using the same interface
  • Data was not reaching SAP CAR

Additionally, the issue was difficult to trace because:

  • No explicit errors were observed
  • Configuration appeared correct and consistent
    Cause
  • The issue occurred after replacing the old PO server with a new server in the ICO configuration.

The scenario was successfully tested in QA without any issues, as the system was still pointing to the old server. This created a false positive validation, and the issue only surfaced in Production after switching to the new server.
QA:

In Production:

  • The configuration was updated to use the new server
  • The issue appeared only after this change

Further analysis revealed that:

  • There were only two ICOs and two sender channels with similar configurations
    These existed because:
  • One set was originally used for the old server
  • Another set was created for the new server configuration
  • After replacing the old server with the new one, both configurations became effectively identical, leading to overlap

Additionally, the interface design included connected flows:

  • One flow handles file pickup and archival in SAP PO
  • Another flow processes and delivers data to SAP CAR

Due to similar sender channel configurations (same server and path, different users), one channel interfered with file pickup. Because of the connected interface design:

  • The file was not picked correctly in the inbound flow
  • As a result, downstream processing to SAP CAR did not occur
  • Since the configurations were nearly identical and no errors were thrown, the issue was not immediately visible.

Solution:

To resolve the issue:

  • Reviewed all sender channels and ICOs for overlapping configurations
  • Identified the duplicate/conflicting sender channel
  • Stopped the unnecessary sender channel
  • Requested the MFT team to resend the SAF file

After implementing the fix:

  • SAP PO successfully picked up the file
  • The archival flow executed correctly
  • The file was processed and delivered to SAP CAR

    Key Takeaways:
  • Avoid maintaining duplicate ICOs and sender channels with identical configurations
  • Ensure clear separation when transitioning from old to new servers
  • Validate end-to-end flows, especially when interfaces are interconnected (archival + processing flows)
  • Always test using the actual target server (Production-like setup)
  • Similar configurations without errors can still cause silent processing conflicts

entry.title: Simplifying ABAP Proxy Migration: From SAP PO to Integration Suite (No MDR Required)
entry.content:
Introduction

This blog presents a complete walkthrough for migrating both outbound and inbound ABAP proxy configurations from SAP PO to SAP Integration Suite (Cloud Integration – CI). It is based on real project experience and focuses on the most direct and efficient path, leveraging SAP’s latest enhancements in ABAP proxy support within Integration Suite.

If you have explored other approaches involving MDR (Metadata Repository), SPXNMIG, or full redesign strategies, this method offers a clear alternative. When the objective is to transition existing proxy scenarios from PO to Integration Suite with minimal disruption, the approach outlined here is both streamlined and practical.

Why this approach — and how it differs from other approaches

There is already substantial guidance available on ABAP proxies, covering areas such as greenfield implementations, MDR-based migrations, OAuth configurations, and pipeline-based architectures in CI. Each of these serves specific use cases effectively.

This blog takes a focused, migration-centric perspective. It outlines a straightforward, end-to-end approach to moving existing proxy scenarios from SAP PO to Integration Suite using SAP’s current ABAP proxy generation capabilities. Both outbound and inbound configurations are addressed together, without introducing MDR or requiring a full pipeline setup. The emphasis is on simplicity, clarity, and direct applicability in migration projects.

Quick Comparison: What Changes, What Stays the Same

 This table shows exactly what changes and what the equivalent looks like after migration:

AspectSAP PO (Before)SAP Integration Suite (After)
Proxy Generation (SAP_PROXY_ESR)Points to SAP PO Enterprise Repository (ESR)Points to host from Process Integration Runtime service key (plan: API) via path prefix /rest/api/v1/workspace/sproxy
Message RoutingRFC destination > SAP PORFC destination > CI (XI Sender iFlow endpoint)
Proxy Visibility in SPROXYService Interfaces from ESR visibleService Interfaces from Cloud Integration packages visible
DependencyESR + SAP PO landscape requiredOnly SAP Integration Suite required
MDR Required?No (ESR is the source)No - new RFC (path prefix) update removes MDR need
Inbound EndpointPO routes to ABAP via internal engineCI > Cloud Connector > /sap/xi/engine in ABAP

Before You Begin — Prerequisites

Ensure the following are in place before starting:

  • Service Interface(s) already imported inside a Cloud Integration Design package (this is what SAP_PROXY_ESR will read from)
  • SAP Cloud Connector (SCC) configured and connected to your BTP subaccount
  • The user for the RFC destination must have the PI_Integration_Developer role collection assigned. For OAuth setup, a Process Integration Runtime service instance (plan: API) with AuthGroup_IntegrationDeveloper role is needed in BTP Cockpit.
  • S/4HANA or ECC system with sufficient basis access to configure SM59, SXMB_ADM, SMICM, SICF, and SPROXY

 

Part 1: Outbound Proxy Migration

Recalling how Outbound Proxy Worked in SAP PO

In SAP PO, outbound proxy communication is handled through two RFC destinations. Understanding both is important, as they map directly to their CI equivalents—only the targets change.

The first RFC destination, typically named SAP_PROXY_ESR, pointed to SAP PO's Enterprise Repository (ESR). Transaction SPROXY used this to browse available Service Interfaces and generate Proxy classes in the ABAP system.

Figure 1: SAP_PROXY_ESR RFC destination pointing to SAP PO's Enterprise Repository (SM59)

The second RFC destination will be configured in SXMB_ADM and handled the actual runtime message routing - every outbound proxy call from ECC/S4 was sent to SAP PO through this destination.

Figure 2: Mapping RFC destination for outbound message routing to SAP PO (SXMB_ADM – Config)

Figure 3: HTTP_PO1 RFC destination — routing messages from S4 to SAP PO (SM59)

Setting Up Outbound Proxy in SAP Integration Suite

What the new setup looks like

The concept is identical in CI — same two RFC destinations, same SXMB_ADM configuration. What changes is only where they point. Let's go through each one.

Figure 4: The outbound Service Interface in SAP PO ESR — this is what we are migrating to CI

Use SAP’s migration tooling (or a third-party alternative) to migrate the Integration Configuration Object (ICO) from PO to CI. After migration, configure the XI Sender adapter address in the iFlow—this becomes the target endpoint for the RFC destination in S/4.

 

Note: The Service Interface must be added manually to the iFlow after ICO migration (Add > Service Interface). It is not included automatically.

Step 1 - RFC Destination for Runtime Message Routing

Create an RFC destination of type G (HTTP connection) in SM59. This destination routes outbound proxy messages from S/4 to the XI Sender endpoint in CI. The path prefix must exactly match the address configured in the XI Sender adapter of the iFlow.

Figure 5: RFC destination for routing outbound messages from S4 to CI (SM59)

Figure 6: The iFlow in CI showing the XI Sender adapter address — this must match the RFC path prefix

 

Best Practice — Centralized Approach: While a direct 1:1 iFlow setup is useful for clarity, a pipeline-based pattern is generally recommended. A single XI Sender iFlow can receive all outbound proxy calls and route them internally using ProcessDirect to interface-specific iFlows. This enables a single RFC destination to serve multiple proxies, significantly reducing configuration overhead.

Step 2 - RFC Destination for Proxy Generation (SAP_PROXY_ESR) — The Key Change

With recent SAP updates, ABAP proxy generation can now be performed directly by connecting the backend system (ECC or S/4) to the SAP Integration Suite tenant.

Once configured, SPROXY reads Service Interfaces directly from CI design packages, enabled via the SAP_PROXY_ESR connection—eliminating the need for MDR or redesign.

Configure the RFC destination in SM59 with:

  • Connection Type: G (HTTP connection)
  • Target Host: Host from the Process Integration Runtime service key (plan type: API) — not the CI tenant host directly
  • Path Prefix: /rest/api/v1/workspace/sproxy
  • SSL: Active (Port 443)

Figure 7: SAP_PROXY_ESR RFC destination now pointing to SAP Integration Suite (SM59)

Step 3 - Authentication for SAP_PROXY_ESR

Before setting up the RFC destination, make sure your user has the PI_Integration_Developer role collection assigned in BTP>users. we have two ways to authenticate and for this blog we're using Basic Auth to keep it simple.

Basic Auth — straightforward, just put the S-User credentials in the Logon & Security tab in SM59. This is what we used in our project.

OAuth — you'll need to first go into BTP Cockpit, create a Process Integration Runtime service instance with plan API, and pick AuthGroup_IntegrationDeveloper during setup. That generates a service key which has everything you need — clientid, clientsecret and token URL. Detailed steps are covered in blog (referred at the end of this blog) on this topic, so I won't repeat it here.

Figure 8: Logon & Security tab — Basic Auth configured with PI_Integration_Developer role (SM59)

Figure 9: RFC destination connection settings — SSL active, port 443 (SM59)

Run the connection test. A response of HTTP 200 confirms the RFC destination is working correctly. Once this is in place, SPROXY will reflect the Service Interfaces available in CI packages.

Figure 10: Service Interface from CI is now visible and ready for proxy generation (SPROXY)

 

Note: Only the package with Service Interfaces within will appear in SPROXY.

Step 4 - Configuring Sender/Receiver IDs and IS_URL in SXMB_ADM

In SXMB_ADM, create the Sender and Receiver IDs that identify the participating systems. These IDs are then referenced in the IS_URL entry, which maps each outbound proxy to its target RFC destination.

Figure 11: SXMB_ADM — Creating Sender/Receiver IDs for the outbound proxy

Configure the IS_URL entry pointing to the RFC destination that routes to CI (e.g., XIMessage_toCI). The Sender/Receiver ID created above is entered as the sub-parameter.

Figure 12: Configure Destination (SXMB_ADM)

Figure 13: IS_URL entry pointing to the CI RFC destination

Once this is configured, trigger a test message from your ABAP program or test tool and confirm it flows correctly through to CI.

 

Tip - If your landscape still has both SAP PO and CI running during the migration phase, each outbound proxy will still need its own Sender/Receiver ID to enable selective routing — some proxies going to PO, others to CI. 

However, all proxies destined for CI can point to a single RFC destination — no need to create one per interface. This works best with a centralized pipeline iFlow, where one XI Sender iFlow receives all outbound proxy calls and routes them internally via ProcessDirect. Individual iFlows per interface would work too, but adds RFC destination or Sender/Receiver ID overhead as interface count grows.

 

Part 2: Inbound Proxy Migration

Inbound proxy scenarios operate in reverse—CI sends messages to the ABAP system, where the inbound proxy processes them. Since the ABAP system is on-premise, secure exposure is handled via SAP Cloud Connector.

Step 1 — Retrieve the ABAP System Hostname (SMICM)

In SMICM → Goto → Services, note the HTTPS hostname and port. This internal host will be mapped in Cloud Connector.

Figure 14: SMICM — Collecting the ABAP system hostname and port for Cloud Connector mapping

Step 2 — Configure Virtual Host Mapping in SAP Cloud Connector

In the Cloud Connector administration portal:

  • Define a Virtual Host (e.g., s4host.internal)
  • Map it to the internal host from SMICM
  • Use HTTPS protocol
  • Set system type as ABAP System

Add resource access:

  • / (full access), or
  • /sap/xi/engine (restricted access)

Then add the resource. For this blog's scenario, access to all paths is granted (resource: /), but for tighter security you can restrict it to /sap/xi/engine specifically.

Figure 15: SAP Cloud Connector — virtual host mapped to the ABAP system

Step 3 — Activate /sap/xi/engine in SICF

In transaction SICF, navigate to the path /sap/xi/engine and check whether the service is active. If it shows as inactive, right-click and activate it.

Figure 16: SICF — /sap/xi/engine confirmed active

 

Watch out - Multi-Client Systems: If your ABAP system has more than one client, the /sap/xi/engine service will default to calling the default client regardless of the URL parameter. To fix this: in SICF, open the /sap/xi/engine service > Logon Data tab > set the Client explicitly to your target client. This is a common gotcha that causes hard-to-diagnose errors.

Step 4 — Construct the Receiver XI Adapter URL in CI

The endpoint URL to be used in the CI Receiver XI Adapter should follows this pattern:

https://<VirtualHost>:<Port>/sap/xi/engine?type=receiver&sap-client=<CLIENT>

Use the virtual host name defined in Cloud Connector (not the internal hostname). This is the URL CI will call to deliver the message to the ABAP system.

Step 5 — Migrate the ICO and Update the Inbound iFlow

Figure 17: The inbound Service Interface in SAP PO ESR — this is what we are migrating to CI

Migrate the ICO from PO to CI using your preferred approach. After migration, open the iFlow and update the Receiver XI Adapter with the URL constructed above. The On-Premise connectivity should be set with the Cloud Connector Location ID.

Figure 18: Migrated iFlow — Receiver XI Adapter updated with the ABAP system URL via Cloud Connector

The Inbound Service Interface also needs to be added to the iFlow separately. It is not pulled in automatically as part of ICO migration.

Figure 19: Inbound Service Interface added separately to the iFlow after migration

Configure the delivery assurance and Quality of Service in the XI adapter based on your scenario requirements.

Step 6 — Activate the Service Interface in SPROXY

Open SPROXY in S/4HANA. The inbound Service Interface will now be visible via SAP_PROXY_ESR. Activate it to generate the corresponding ABAP proxy class.

Figure 20: SPROXY — Inbound Service Interface visible from CI, activated for proxy generation

Once activated, test the end-to-end flow: send a test message from CI and verify it is received and processed by the ABAP inbound proxy. Check SXMB_MONI in the ABAP system for message status.

 

Troubleshooting Guide

Below are the most common issues encountered during proxy migration, along with their root causes and fixes. This is based on real project experience and commonly reported issues in the community

SymptomLikely CauseFix
Connection test on SAP_PROXY_ESR returns HTTP 404using CI endpoint or wrong path prefix (path prefix is case sensitive)Verify the path prefix is correct. Also ensure the target host in the service key is the host from the Process Integration Runtime (plan: API) and not the CI tenant host directly.
Service Interface not showing up in SPROXYService Interface not inside a CI package, missed manual import of Service Interface after IFlow migrationCheck Service Interface is inside CI package
Outbound proxy message not reaching CIIS_URL entry in SXMB_ADM pointing to wrong destination or Sender/Receiver ID mismatchCross check the IS_URL mapping — namespace in Sender/Receiver ID must exactly match the proxy namespace
Inbound message from CI hitting wrong client/sap/xi/engine defaulting to system default clientIn SICF, set the explicit Logon Data client on /sap/xi/engine service

 

Summary

Migrating ABAP proxy scenarios from SAP PO to SAP Integration Suite does not have to be complicated. Here is the core of what this blog covers:

  • The SAP_PROXY_ESR RFC destination is the linchpin of this approach. By pointing it to Integration Suite instead of the ESR, SPROXY automatically reads Service Interfaces from CI packages — no MDR, no SPXNMIG, no inline type conversion needed.
  • For Outbound Proxy: update two RFC destinations (SAP_PROXY_ESR and the message routing destination in SXMB_ADM) to point to CI instead of PO. The rest of the SXMB_ADM Sender/Receiver ID and IS_URL config works the same way.
  • For Inbound Proxy: expose the ABAP system's /sap/xi/engine endpoint via Cloud Connector, configure the Receiver XI Adapter in your CI iFlow, and activate the Service Interface in SPROXY.
  • Watch out for: wrong client in SICF (multi-client systems), the target host for RFC: SAP_PROXY_ESR is from the Process Integration Runtime service key and not the CI tenant URL directly, and Service Interface not appearing in SPROXY (package not imported into CI).
Related Reading: For OAuth 2.0 setup with SAP_PROXY_ESR: "ABAP Proxy generation support with SAP Integration Suite" on SAP Community & ABAP Proxy Generation - General Procedure | SAP Help Portal on SAP Help Portal. For MDR-based migration: "Efficient ABAP Proxy Migration from SAP PO to Integration Suite" on SAP Community.

 

Thanks for reading. Questions or corrections — drop them in the comments, I'll do my best to help.

entry.title: Middleware Isn't Dead. It Grew Up.
entry.content:
The recent online conversation sparked by SAP's strategic investment in n8n has been energetic, and largely for the right reasons. The excitement is warranted. The investment is significant. But some of what's circulating online conflates a few things that are worth separating clearly — and some of the most important parts of the story are getting lost in the noise.

This post is my attempt to clear that up.

 

What the n8n partnership actually is

At SAP Sapphire 2026, SAP announced a strategic investment in n8n — the open-source workflow automation platform — as part of a multi-year commercial partnership with deep product alignment.

This is a genuine strategic move, and the reason is worth stating plainly: SAP didn't partner with n8n to acquire a tool. SAP partnered with n8n to gain access to a community. n8n brings 1.7 million active builders, 1,000+ app and system integrations, and a thriving ecosystem of workflows and templates built by people who were never traditional SAP developers. That's a different builder profile — technical generalists, citizen developers, automation engineers — and it's exactly the kind of expansion the SAP developer ecosystem has long needed. You no longer need to know ABAP or CDS views to build useful business automations.

For practitioners, what this means in practice is a visual, node-based workflow canvas embedded alongside the agent and app-building capabilities in Joule Studio, SAP's unified agent-building, app development, and automation environment within the SAP Business AI Platform. Builders who live in automation-first tools will feel immediately at home. The possibilities for connecting SAP agents to external services and building agentic workflows visually are genuinely compelling.

As we look to the future, expect SAP to continue to deepen this partnership. n8n's reach across the SAP landscape will grow, but more on that direction as it develops.

What the n8n partnership is not

Here is where some of the online commentary has gone sideways.

n8n in Joule Studio is a workflow automation and agent orchestration layer. SAP Integration Suite is an enterprise integration backbone. They solve fundamentally different problems, and treating one as a substitute for the other creates real architectural risk.

Integration Suite handles the things that have to work every time, at scale, under governance: enterprise-grade process integration, B2B EDI and trading partner management, full API lifecycle from design through monetization, hybrid and sovereign deployment through Edge Integration Cell, enterprise-grade event streaming, end-to-end error handling, SLA management, and audit trails for business-critical process flows. These are the scenarios where a visual workflow canvas is a complement, not a substitute.

The more useful frame is this: Joule Studio is where you build the agent, the app, or the workflow. Integration Suite is what lets those components reach every system, every process, and every partner across your enterprise — securely and at scale. The Joule Studio positioning is explicit about this: Integration Suite is named as one of the foundational layers that makes agents enterprise-ready. The two together are additive, and practitioners are better off for it.

The differing viewpoints in the online conversation are healthy

A range of perspectives has surfaced in these discussions — some overstating what n8n changes, some appropriately cautious about what it doesn't yet do. That kind of discourse sharpens everyone's thinking. But a few misconceptions keep appearing, and the most important one to address is the idea that n8n's arrival in Joule Studio resolves the PI/PO question.

It doesn't. Not yet, and not for most scenarios.

The PI/PO clock is real

SAP Process Integration and Process Orchestration reach end of standard maintenance in 2027, with extended maintenance available through 2030. That date is not moving.

The vast majority of PI/PO workloads are traditional integration scenarios — system-to-system message routing, B2B document exchange, ABAP proxy patterns, IDoc flows, RFC and JDBC lookups — that map directly and logically to SAP Integration Suite. These are not workflow automation scenarios. Migration tooling for these patterns exists today: the Migration Assessment tool is available on the free tier of Integration Suite and can give you a complete inventory and effort estimate of your PI/PO landscape without any commitment. The Migration Tool in Cloud Integration handles the conversion for the most common adapter patterns.

If you haven't started making a plan to migrate off PI/PO, it's not too late — but it's getting there. A large landscape with 300+ interfaces can take a year or more even with the best tooling. The time to start assessing is now, not when the maintenance window starts closing.

The good news: that migration is about to get meaningfully faster. SAP announced the PI/PO Migration Agent at Sapphire 2026, with general availability targeted for Q3 2026. This agent brings AI-driven automation to the medium and high complexity migrations that previously required the most specialist effort — the ones involving custom code, complex mappings, and logic that the existing Migration Tool couldn't handle automatically. For landscapes where migration friction has been the primary blocker, this agent compresses the execution phase significantly.

If you haven't started your assessment yet, there's no reason to wait. SAP's Migration Factory offers a free migration assessment to help you understand the scope, complexity, and effort of your PI/PO landscape before you commit to anything. Apply for your free assessment here.

The bigger picture

The n8n investment, the PI/PO Migration Agent, the MCP Gateway reaching general availability this quarter, the Joule conversational interface coming to Integration Suite in Q3 — these aren't separate announcements. They're part of a coherent direction: an integration platform that is becoming intelligent from the inside, connected to the entire enterprise, and accessible to a much broader builder community than ever before.

More tools. More flexibility. More paths to get your integration and automation landscape where it needs to be.

The middleware argument hasn't been killed. It's been answered — with options.

entry.title: An XI (ABAP Proxy) Sender Simulator for SAP Integration Testing
entry.content:
Introduction

Have you ever wanted to test one inbound ABAP Proxy interface, but before sending one single message you first had to prepare a PI, PO, or SAP Cloud Integration flow?

I have run into this many times.

Sometimes I only want to answer a simple question: can this SAP system receive this XI message, and does the payload match the expected interface? But the setup ends up bigger than the test itself. You may need a sender flow, a receiver channel, routing, credentials, certificates, sample payloads, and sometimes help from another team.

For daily development, SAP AIF testing, and incident analysis, this is slow.

So I built a small local tool: an XI (ABAP Proxy) Sender Simulator.

It sends SAP XI 3.0 multipart messages directly to the ABAP XI Engine endpoint. 

The goal is not to replace middleware. The goal is to make local testing and troubleshooting faster.

Where the tool sits

In a normal landscape, a client system reaches the ABAP inbound proxy through CPI / PI / PO. The simulator skips that whole sender flow and talks straight to the XI engine on the receiver:

This is not a replacement for the real middleware path. It is a focused shortcut for the cases where you only need to test the receiver side.

Why I built it

This idea is not new for me. I wanted to build this kind of tool many years ago.

The pain was already clear. I often needed a quick way to send one XI message to one SAP system, especially when working on SAP AIF and ABAP Proxy interfaces. I knew a small sender simulator would save time.

But I never had enough time to build it properly.

AI coding assistants change that. AI does not replace SAP integration knowledge. I still need to understand XI 3.0, ABAP Proxy, AIF, payload namespaces, QoS, authentication, and how to test all of it. But AI helps a lot with implementation, refactoring, tests, UI work, and documentation.

It lets me finish ideas I had for years but could not complete before because of limited time and energy. This tool is one of them.

What the tool does

The tool gives you a local web UI for sending XI 3.0 messages.

The basic flow is simple:

  1. Enter the SAP XI Engine URL and user.
  2. Enter sender and receiver routing information.
  3. Paste or choose a WSDL.
  4. Parse the WSDL.
  5. Generate a sample payload.
  6. Edit the payload.
  7. Send the XI message.
  8. Check the SAP response and local history.

Visually, one round-trip looks like this:

The tool builds the XI 3.0 request for you:

  • XI SOAP envelope
  • message ID
  • sender and receiver party / component
  • interface namespace and name
  • QoS mode
  • multipart/related HTTP body
  • payload cid: reference

Then it sends the request to an endpoint like:

/sap/xi/engine?type=receiver&sap-client=<client>

How it works

An XI 3.0 HTTP request is a multipart/related message.

It contains two main parts:

  • Part 1: the XI SOAP envelope, with protocol and routing metadata.
  • Part 2: the business payload XML.

The SOAP envelope references the payload by cid:.  Visually:

The tool reads the WSDL and pulls out the information it needs:

  • service interface name
  • interface namespace
  • request payload element
  • payload namespace
  • synchronous or asynchronous mode

For asynchronous interfaces the tool uses ExactlyOnce. For synchronous interfaces it uses BestEffort. The tool decides this from the WSDL operation: if the operation has an output message, it treats it as synchronous.

This WSDL parsing is important. In real SAP projects, the service interface namespace and the payload message type namespace are not always the same. Mixing them up leads to errors like INTERFACE_REGISTRATION_ERROR or INTERFACE_SIGNATURE_ERROR.

If you want to dig into the wire format itself (every field in the SOAP envelope, what type=receiver does, how to read <SAP:Error> codes), I keep my own working notes here: docs/xi-protocol.md. Those are not official SAP documentation, just what I have learned from debugging.

When it is useful

This tool is useful when you want to:

  • test an inbound ABAP Proxy interface quickly
  • reproduce an SAP AIF inbound issue
  • check whether the interface namespace and name are correct
  • check whether the payload root element and namespace are correct
  • generate a first sample payload from a WSDL
  • separate transport / protocol errors from application errors
  • do a quick regression test without rebuilding a full middleware flow

The main value is a shorter feedback loop.

Try it

GitHub https://github.com/LF-LLL/xi-abap-proxy-sender-simulator

Safety and scope

This tool is not an official SAP tool.

It is not delivered, supported, or endorsed by SAP.

It is not designed for production message processing.

It should not be used as a production integration component, retry tool, or monitoring tool.

It is a local development and testing helper. The target users are developers, integration consultants, and operations / support colleagues who need to validate or reproduce integration messages more efficiently.

The tool can send authenticated HTTP requests to SAP systems, so it has some safety boundaries:

  • It listens on 127.0.0.1 by default.
  • It refuses non-localhost binding unless the user explicitly opts in.
  • It uses a per-start token to reduce accidental local or cross-site calls.
  • It only accepts send URLs whose path looks like a SAP endpoint, such as /sap/... or /XISOAPAdapter/....
  • It does not return password defaults from the local config file back to the browser.
  • It does not store passwords in history.
  • It redacts sensitive response headers.
  • It truncates large payloads and responses before storing them in local history.

Even with all of that, please treat it as a lab tool. Run it only on your own machine, or in a controlled test environment.

entry.title: Migrating Interfaces with Dynamic Configuration (ASMA) from SAP PO to SAP Integration Suite
entry.content:
Migrating Interfaces with Dynamic Configuration (ASMA) from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite 

This article explains how to migrate integration interfaces that rely on Dynamic Configuration (Adapter-Specific Message Attributes, ASMA) from SAP Process Orchestration (PO) to SAP Cloud Integration. It covers the technical root cause, a practical step-by-step migration approach, and the PO library dependencies involved. 

What Is ASMA (Adapter-Specific Message Attributes)? 

When running integration scenarios in SAP Process Orchestration, integration developers often need to pass dynamic, context-specific values — such as a target filename, a dynamic URL path, or a SOAP action — from the sender adapter through the integration logic to a receiver adapter. The mechanism that enables this in SAP PO is called Adapter-Specific Message Attributes (ASMA). 

ASMA values are carried in a special container called Dynamic Configuration, which travels with the message throughout the SAP PO pipeline. They can be read and written in three ways: 

  1. UDF in Message Mapping: In User-Defined Functions (UDFs) within a message mapping using the Java API: DynamicConfiguration, DynamicConfigurationKey, StreamTransformationConstants.DYNAMIC_CONFIGURATION. 
  2. Java Mapping: In a standalone Java Mapping class that extends AbstractTransformation, using input.getDynamicConfiguration() to read or write ASMA values directly on the TransformationInput object. 
  3. XSLT Mapping: Via the SAP XI Mapping API extension functions provided by the SAP XML Toolkit. These extension functions allow an XSLT stylesheet to call into the Dynamic Configuration container to read and write ASMA values at runtime. 

Core API Dependencies for Dynamic Configuration 

Dynamic Configuration API depends on two specific JAR files that are part of the Process Orchestration runtime.  

JAR File 

Key Classes Provided 

Purpose 

com.sap.xpi.ib.mapping.lib.jar 

AbstractTransformation, TransformationInput, TransformationOutput, StreamTransformationException, AbstractTrace 

Core mapping framework. All Java Mappings must extend AbstractTransformation and implement the transform() method. 

com.sap.xi.mapping.tool.lib_api.jar 

DynamicConfiguration, DynamicConfigurationKey, StreamTransformationConstants 

Dynamic Configuration API. Provides the typed container for reading and writing Adapter-Specific Message Attributes by namespace/attribute key. 

 

So, how to migrate an Interface with ASMA Using the SAP Integration Suite capability? 

1. Create a Data Extraction in Migration Assessment (https://help.sap.com/docs/integration-suite/sap-integration-suite/migration-assessment) 

Run Migration Assessment first to connect to your SAP PO system, extract all integration artifacts, and evaluate each scenario. As we will explore in this post, extracting this data reveals both the complexity and the use of Dynamic Configuration. 

Rules identified: 

  • GMMCustomUDFUsageCount 
  • GMMCustomUDFDynamicConfiguration 
  • JAVAMDynamicConfiguration 

 2. Migration Tooling (https://help.sap.com/docs/integration-suite/sap-integration-suite/migration-tooling?q=migration+tool) 

Using the assessment results as input, proceed with the Migration Tool for scenarios classified as "Ready to migrate" or "Adjustment required." The tool semi-automatically generates iFlows in SAP Integration Suite based on templates derived from the SAP PO configuration.  

3.Outcome & Validation 

After the migration, validate the migrated iFlows. The combined use of both tools ensures a structured, risk-reduced, and cost-efficient transition from SAP PO/PI to SAP Integration Suite. 

What Happens When You Migrate the Interfaces with ASMA 

Let's have a look at this demo scenario: 

 

1. Request Payload 

2. Processing Logic 

  1. Java mapping reads the input message, gets "action" and puts it into Dynamic Configuration attribute "THeaderSOAPACTION". 
  2. XSLT Mapping converts the input into message into target format and store tag "message" into Dynamic Configuration attribute "inputMessage". 
  3. Receiver Communication Channel sets the Dynamic Configuration attribute "THeaderSOAPACTION" into SOAPAction. 
  4. Once the target system processes the message, there is a Graphical Mapping with “User Defined Functions (UDF)”. This function assign values coming from Dynamic Configuration Attributes, "THeaderSOAPACTION" and "inputMessage", and puts into the tags "dynAction" and "inputMessage" respectivelly. 

 3. Response Payload 

 

Once the interface is migrated, you will find in your Integration Suite package the artifacts generated based on your SAP PO objects. 

Check the Interface (flow). You will see boxes representing the logic that was defined on your SAP PO with wrapper functions depending on your ASMA use case.  

 

JAVA MAPPING (Using Dynamic Configuration) – A wrapper class is generated by the Migration tool by default to provide temporary compatibility. While you can override the Java method to retain Dynamic Configuration logic, this approach is not recommended for production use. The preferred approach is to replace the Dynamic Configuration calls with message headers as described in the adaptation section below. 

 XSLT MAPPING (Using Dynamic Configuration) - The migrated XSLT artifact retains the SAP XI Mapping API calls. These must be adapted to use Cloud Integration-native header access mechanisms. 

GRAPHICAL MAPPING (Using Dynamic Configuration) - UDFs referencing the Dynamic Configuration API are migrated as-is and will require manual adaptation. 

 

 

How to Adapt ASMA-Based Interfaces for Cloud Integration 

Evaluate your scenario — Identify all ASMA usages across Java Mappings, UDFs, and XSLT stylesheets. The Migration tool does not replace Dynamic Configuration logic. 

Understand how messages are processed by Cloud Integration. "Dynamic Values” are passed via named message headers or properties (set by a Content Modifier or Groovy Script step) not via a Dynamic Configuration container. 

 

 In SAP Cloud Integration, the correct mechanism for passing dynamic values through an integration flow is via message headers or exchange properties. These are set in dedicated flow steps before the mapping executes and then referenced in the mapping logic or adapter configuration. 

 

Concept 

SAP PO (Examples) 

SAP Cloud Integration (Examples) 

Dynamic value container 

  • Dynamic Configuration (ASMA) 
  • Message Headers 
  • Exchange Properties 

How values are set 

  • Java DynamicConfiguration.put() 
  • Content Modifier 
  • Groovy Script setProperty() / setHeaders() 

How values are read in mapping 

  • Java DynamicConfiguration.get() 
  • Content Modifier 
  • Graphical Mapping out-of-the-box functions to getProperty and getHeader 
  • Groovy Script getProperty() / getHeaders() 

Dynamic adapter config 

  • Adapter reads ASMA by namespace + attribute key 
  • Adapter uses expression ${header.HEADER_NAME} or ${property.PROPERTY_NAME} 

 

Therefore, if an imported mapping uses Dynamic Configuration APIs for accessing Adapter-Specific Message Attributes, the integration flow must be manually adjusted to ensure correct execution.  

 

References 

Links 

Creating Message Mapping as an Artifact 

https://help.sap.com/docs/integration-suite/sap-integration-suite/developing-message-mapping-as-artifact?locale=en-US 

Headers and Exchange Properties Provided by the Integration Framework 

https://help.sap.com/docs/cloud-integration/sap-cloud-integration/headers-and-exchange-properties-provided-by-integration-framework 

Access Headers and Properties in Scripts 

https://help.sap.com/docs/integration-suite/sap-integration-suite/access-headers-and-properties-in-scripts 

 

 

Let's Review the Integration Flow Imported in the Previous Steps and Look into Adaptations 

 

 1. Java Mapping Replacement: A Content Modifier step is added before the mapping to set the SOAPAction message header and store the inputMessage value into message property. This replaces the Dynamic Configuration to write operations previously performed in Java Mapping. 

 

 2. XSLT Mapping: Remove Dynamic Configuration functionalities 

 

 3. Graphical Mapping: UDFs adapted to use out-of-the-box functions instead of the Dynamic Configuration API. 

 

 

 

 Additionally, for XI Adapter, Natively Supports ASMA 

The XI adapter in Cloud Integration natively supports Adapter-Specific Message Attributes. The XI sender adapter automatically creates a pair of exchange properties for each ASMA: one holding the value and one holding the namespace. When configuring ASMAs for the XI receiver adapter, both properties must be explicitly created. 

For scenarios using the XI adapter, the migration of ASMA-based logic can therefore be automated. For other adapter types, a similar approach applies, with the key distinction that the namespace property is typically not required. It is specifically needed by the XI receiver adapter, but not by other adapters. 

In pipeline-based integration approaches this is handled automatically within the generic XI inbound and XI outbound flows. Since exchange properties are not passed between flows, corresponding headers are created at the XI inbound step and then converted back to properties at the XI outbound step. 

For further details, see: 

References 

Links 

Generic Inbound and Outbound

Summary 

Migrating integration scenarios that use Dynamic Configuration (ASMA) from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite requires a multi-step approach.

entry.title: Enhanced Landscape and Cost Estimation in Migration Assessment
entry.content:
One of the most critical aspects of planning a migration from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite is understanding the real message consumption and performance characteristics of your existing landscape. Accurate sizing and license forecasting depend on granular and reliable metrics.

Until now, Migration Assessment provided message throughput data based on a fixed 30-day collection window, which was presented alongside the evaluation results in the Excel report. While this was useful for initial planning, customers consistently needed more flexibility in data collection periods, extended historical visibility for trend analysis, and direct metrics that could serve as input for SAP Integration Suite license simulations.

With this enhancement, we are expanding the message analysis capabilities of Migration Assessment to provide a dedicated, comprehensive view of message throughput and performance data. This includes configurable time ranges for performance data collection, extended message volume analysis over 1, 3, and 6-month periods, and calculated fields that directly map to SAP Integration Suite message metrics, enabling you to build accurate cost estimations for your target landscape.

Moreover, although Migration Assessment does not provide direct calculations for underlying components such as SAP Advanced Event Mesh (AEM) or SAP Edge Integration Cell (EIC) — since the respective sizing tools may change at any time, the output provided in the report can be compiled and used as input for those subsequent tools.

What Changed

This enhancement introduces changes across multiple areas of the Migration Assessment tool:

  • Data Extraction: A new configurable time range for performance data collection.
  • Test Connection: New connectivity checks for Message Monitor and Performance Monitor.
  • Excel Report: A new dedicated “Message Analysis” tab consolidating all message and performance metrics with calculated SAP Integration Suite message metrics.
  • Dashboard: Updated message throughput fields reflecting the extended collection periods.
  • PDF Report: Replacement of TOP 10 message throughput for a executive-level summary.

The following sections describe each change in detail.

Data Extraction: Performance Data Collection Time Range

When creating a new Data Extraction request, a new option is now available: Performance Data Collection – Time Range. This setting controls the time interval used to query the Performance Monitor API on your SAP Process Orchestration system.

The available options are:

  • Yesterday: Collects performance data for the previous day (D-1) using hourly aggregation intervals.
  • Last Week: Collects performance data for the last 7-day period using weekly aggregation.
  • Last Month: Collects performance data for the last 30-day period using monthly aggregation.

By default, “Yesterday” is selected. This value determines how the performance metrics (message size, processing time, and message count) are collected and labeled in the final report.

 

Please Note: Ensure the selected time range is available in your SAP Process Orchestration system’s Performance Monitor. This setting applies only to Java components. If the Performance Monitor does not have data for the selected interval, the extraction will proceed, but performance metrics will not be included in the final report. Always review the extraction logs to confirm successful data collection.

Test Connection: New Connectivity Checks

The Test Connection feature has been extended with two new connectivity checks, providing visibility into whether the required monitoring APIs are accessible before running a data extraction.

Message Monitor

A new test row validates connectivity to the Message Monitor API. Upon execution, the tool retrieves and displays the list of XI Components available in the system.

The result can be:

  • Success: The API returned the component list successfully. The message “Operation Completed Successfully” is displayed.
  • Warning (No Components): The API responded, but no components were returned. A warning is displayed: “No components were returned by the API. Please ensure the user has the necessary permissions to access this information.”
  • Warning (API Failure): The API call failed, and the error details are shown.

In case of a warning, an additional disclaimer is displayed: “If message metrics for the Message Monitor cannot be captured, they will not be included in the final report.”

In all cases (including success), the following informational note is displayed: “To capture general message throughput for synchronous messages, enable synchronous message logging in SAP NetWeaver Administrator (NWA). Note that enabling message logging introduces additional load on the database server, as described in SAP Note 2442373.”

Performance Monitor (Java)

A second new test row validates connectivity to the Performance Monitor API. Similar to the Message Monitor check, it retrieves and displays the list of available Java components.

The result follows the same logic as the Message Monitor check: Success, Warning (No Components), or Warning (API Failure), with the corresponding disclaimer for warning cases: “If message metrics for the Performance Monitor cannot be captured, they will not be included in the final report.”

Excel Report: New Message Analysis Tab

Previously, message throughput and performance metrics were included as additional columns in the “Eval by Integration Scenario” sheet. With this enhancement, these metrics have been moved to a dedicated new sheet called Message Analysis, positioned after the “Scenario Technical Details” tab. This provides a cleaner separation between evaluation results and landscape/sizing data.

The following columns have been removed from the “Eval by Integration Scenario” sheet:

  • Message Throughput (30 Days)
  • Average Message Size in Bytes (30 Days)
  • Average Message Processing Time in Milliseconds (30 Days)
  • Maximum Message Size in Bytes (30 Days)

Message Analysis Sheet

The new Message Analysis sheet consolidates all message throughput, performance, and calculated SAP Integration Suite metrics in a single view. The column labels are dynamically generated based on the actual dates and time ranges of the collected data.

The sheet contains the following columns:

  • Type: Indicates whether the interface is an “Integrated Configuration” (ICO) or “Receiver Determination” (RD).
  • Integration Scenario: Interface identification using the standard naming convention: SenderParty|SenderComponent|SenderInterface|SenderInterfaceNamespace|ReceiverParty|ReceiverComponent.
  • Interface Type: Indicates whether the interface is Synchronous or Asynchronous.
  • T-Shirt Size: T-Shirt size derived from the total weight according to the defined SAP intervals.

Message Monitor Metrics

  • Message Throughput 1 Month (dynamic date range): Message volume collected from Message Monitor for the most recent 1-month period. The date range is calculated dynamically and displayed in the column header.
  • Message Throughput 3 Months (dynamic date range): Message volume aggregated across three consecutive monthly intervals. If fewer than three months of data are available, the tool uses whatever is accessible and logs a corresponding message.
  • Message Throughput 6 Months (dynamic date range): Message volume aggregated across six consecutive monthly intervals. If fewer than six months of data are available, the tool uses whatever is accessible and logs a corresponding message.

Performance Monitor Metrics

  • Message Count (dynamic): Total message count retrieved from the Performance Monitor API. The label reflects the time range selected during data extraction (with actual dates displayed).
  • Average Message Size in Bytes (dynamic): Average message payload size from Performance Monitor for the selected time range.
  • Average Message Processing Time in Milliseconds (dynamic): Average processing time per message from Performance Monitor.
  • Maximum Message Size in Bytes (dynamic): Maximum observed message size from Performance Monitor.
  • Messages per Second (dynamic): Calculated field based on the Performance Monitor message count divided by the number of seconds in the selected period (Yesterday: /86,400; Last Week: /604,800; Last Month: /2,592,000).

SAP Integration Suite Calculated Metrics

  • SAP Integration Suite – Average Message Metric Multiplier (250kb): Calculated as Average Message Size / 250,000 (rounded up to integer). Reflects how SAP Integration Suite counts messages based on the 250kb message size threshold.
  • SAP Integration Suite Message Metric (1 Month): Message Throughput (1 Month) multiplied by the Average Message Metric Multiplier.
  • SAP Integration Suite Message Metric (3 Months): Message Throughput (3 Months) multiplied by the Average Message Metric Multiplier.
  • SAP Integration Suite Message Metric (6 Months): Message Throughput (6 Months) multiplied by the Average Message Metric Multiplier.

Please Note: If the Average Message Size is zero but message throughput data exists (in any of the 1, 3, or 6-month periods), the multiplier defaults to 1 to ensure a minimum message metric is reported.

Message throughput and performance metrics may vary between Message Monitor and Performance Monitor depending on the system configuration, monitoring features, and available logging data in SAP Process Orchestration. Therefore, the selected source for the analysis baseline may influence subsequent sizing, migration, and architectural assessments. It is recommended to validate the extraction logs to ensure the data was collected successfully and without inconsistencies, and check the data directly in the SAP Process Orchestration system if necessary.

Dashboard: Updated Message Throughput Fields

The Scenario Evaluation dashboard has been updated to reflect the extended message throughput collection. The interface-level detail now displays the Message Throughput for 1 Month, 3 Months, and 6 Months, providing a quick visual overview of message volume trends directly from the dashboard without needing to export the Excel report.

PDF Report: Message Throughput Analysis

The PDF report has been redesigned to provide a more useful executive-level summary regarding message throughput. The previous “Messages Processed (Top 10)” page has been replaced with a new Message Throughput Analysis section that provides context and guidance without attempting to replicate the full data set.

The new section communicates the following key points:

  • A comprehensive analysis of message throughput and system performance was conducted to support landscape evaluation, migration planning, and architectural decision-making.
  • The complete results, including interface-level breakdowns and SAP Integration Suite metric simulations, are available in the Message Analysis tab of the Excel report.
  • Performance and throughput metrics depend on the monitoring and logging capabilities enabled in SAP Process Orchestration at the time of extraction.
  • SAP Note 3300008 should be implemented for enhanced performance data collection (message size and processing time).
  • Synchronous message throughput requires synchronous message logging to be enabled in NWA (SAP Note 2442373).
  • It is strongly recommended to review the extraction logs and validate results directly in the SAP Process Orchestration system.

How This Helps Your Migration Planning

With these new capabilities, the Migration Assessment now provides a complete picture for landscape and cost estimation:

  • License Forecasting: The SAP Integration Suite Message Metric columns give you a direct input for license sizing. By examining the 1-month, 3-month, and 6-month trends, you can account for seasonal variations and growth patterns in your message consumption.
  • Architectural Decisions: The Messages per Second metric, combined with message size data, enables you to evaluate whether specific interfaces require Edge Integration Cell deployment or can be handled entirely in the cloud runtime.
  • Sizing for Additional Components: Although Migration Assessment does not calculate sizing for components such as SAP Advanced Event Mesh or Edge Integration Cell directly, the raw metrics provided (message count, message size, throughput rates) serve as direct input to the respective sizing tools.
  • Trend Analysis: Comparing 1-month, 3-month, and 6-month volumes helps identify inactive interfaces (candidates for decommission), interfaces with growing traffic (requiring attention during migration), and seasonal patterns that should influence go-live timing.

Conclusion

This enhancement transforms Migration Assessment from a purely technical migration-readiness tool into a comprehensive landscape analysis and cost estimation platform. By consolidating message throughput, performance metrics, and SAP Integration Suite license calculations into a single, dedicated report sheet, you now have the data foundation needed to build accurate business cases, perform license simulations, and make informed architectural decisions for your SAP Integration Suite migration.

We recommend running a new data extraction with the updated tool to take advantage of these capabilities. Review the Test Connection results beforehand to ensure your system’s monitoring APIs are accessible, and always validate the extraction logs to confirm complete and consistent data collection.

Additional References

  • SAP Note 3300008 – Performance Data Collection for Migration Assessment
  • SAP Note 2442373 – Synchronous Message Logging in NWA
  • SAP Note 2942344 – Definition of a Message on SAP Integration Suite
  • Using Migration Assessment to Plan Your SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite Migration
  • FAQ – Migration from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite
  • From PI/PO to SAP Edge Integration Cell – Initial Sizing Approach
  • Get Started with Migration to SAP Integration Suite (Discovery Center Mission)
