entry.title: Migration Analytics: Enhanced Migration Trend and Rule Insights in Migration Assessment
entry.content:
One of the key challenges in planning a migration from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite is understanding the true complexity behind each integration scenario. While the Migration Assessment already provides a consolidated migration status per interface, a single classification often oversimplifies the real distribution of effort across your landscape.

In practice, most interfaces are not purely "migratable" or "non-migratable". They consist of a combination of elements: some can be automatically migrated, some require partial adaptation, and others demand deeper evaluation and redesign.

With this enhancement, we are introducing a migration trend per ICO, enriched with rule-level insights, migration tool coverage indicators, and effort distribution analysis. The Migration Assessment now provides a more analytical and insight-driven view that enables stakeholders to answer critical questions: How complex is the migration? What portion can be automated? Where are the main blockers? How should we prioritize? How is my landscape affected per technical dependencies?

Moreover, this update introduces the concept of Migration Tool Coverage, which clearly distinguishes between capabilities covered by SAP migration tooling and those requiring manual intervention, a key factor for estimating timelines, resource needs, and overall project risk.

What Changed

This enhancement introduces changes across multiple areas of the Migration Assessment tool:

  • Dashboard: New analytical charts providing migration readiness distribution, tool coverage overview, rule impact analysis, and effort concentration.
  • Filter and Integration Scenarios: A new filter field for Migration Tool Coverage and additional columns in the scenario evaluation table.
  • Setting Rules: New rule attributes for "Analytics-Relevant" and "Migration Tool Coverage" visibility in the configuration page.
  • Excel Report: New columns in the Full Evaluation Results and Eval by Integration Scenario tabs reflecting migration readiness percentages and tool coverage.
  • PDF Report: A new Migration Analytics Overview section with charts and tables summarizing readiness, tool coverage, rule impact, and effort distribution.

The following sections describe each change in detail.

Dashboard: New Analytical Charts and Filters

The Scenario Evaluation dashboard has been significantly enhanced with new analytical visualizations that provide a deeper understanding of the migration landscape. These new charts complement the existing assessment summary by offering rule-level and effort-level insights.

Overall Landscape Migration Readiness

A new pie chart displays the average migration readiness distribution across all assessed integration scenarios, broken down into three categories: Ready to Migrate, Adjustment Required, and Evaluation Required. Each scenario's contribution is weighted by its triggered rules, and the chart aggregates these percentages across the entire landscape to provide an overall migration readiness profile.

This chart answers the fundamental question: across my entire landscape, what proportion of migration effort falls into each category? Rather than counting interfaces by their final status, it reflects the weighted distribution of complexity within each interface.

Migration Tool Coverage by Scenarios

A second new pie chart shows integration scenarios grouped by the extent to which SAP migration tooling can support their migration. Scenarios are classified into four levels: Low (up to 30%), Medium (up to 60%), High (up to 80%), and Very High (above 80%).

This chart helps stakeholders gauge the overall automation potential of the landscape and identify where manual intervention will be required.

Additional Filter: Migration Tool Coverage

A new filter field for Migration Tool Coverage has been added to the dashboard, allowing users to narrow down the scenario list by automation potential.

This enables focused analysis on specific segments of the landscape, such as scenarios with low tool coverage that may require additional planning.

Integration Scenario Table: New Columns

The integration scenario evaluation table now includes additional columns reflecting the migration readiness breakdown per interface:

  • Migration Readiness (Ready to Migrate): Percentage of the interface's rules weighted toward automatic migration.
  • Migration Readiness (Adjustment Required): Percentage weighted toward adaptation needs.
  • Migration Readiness (Evaluation Required): Percentage weighted toward deeper evaluation.
  • Migration Tool Coverage: Indicates the level of SAP migration tooling support for the interface.

These columns provide per-interface transparency into the migration trend, going beyond the single consolidated status to reveal the underlying distribution of effort.

TOP 10 Scenarios Impacted by Distinct Rules

Three new horizontal bar charts have been added, one per assessment category (Ready to Migrate, Adjustment Required, Evaluation Required). Each chart displays the top 10 rules that impact the highest number of integration scenarios within that category. Rules are identified by their sub-characteristic or value (for adapters and modules, the specific value is used rather than the generic sub-characteristic) and sorted by the number of impacted scenarios.

Only analytics-relevant rules are included in these charts — rules flagged as irrelevant for analytical purposes (such as structural rules like ICOReceivers) are excluded to ensure the visualization highlights the most meaningful technical characteristics driving the assessment outcome.

Overall Effort (Weight) Concentration by Rules

A new Pareto-style chart displays the cumulative effort distribution across assessment rules. Each bar represents a rule's total weight contribution to the overall migration effort, while a cumulative line tracks the running percentage toward 100%. Rules are sorted by their total effort impact (not individual weight), helping identify the critical few rules that account for the majority of migration complexity.

This chart enables project teams to quickly identify where the bulk of migration effort is concentrated, supporting targeted decision-making about which technical areas to address first for maximum impact.

Setting Rules: Analytics-Relevant and Migration Tool Coverage

The rule configuration page (Configure > Rules) has been extended with two new attributes that control how rules participate in the new analytical features:

  • Analytics-Relevant (Yes/No): Determines whether a rule is included in the analytical charts (TOP 10 rule impact charts). Rules that are structural or always present (such as ICOReceivers, RequestMessageType, ResponseMessageType) can be marked as not analytics-relevant to avoid skewing the visualization.
  • Migration Tool Coverage (Yes/No): Indicates whether the capability assessed by this rule is covered by SAP migration tooling. This attribute drives the Migration Tool Coverage calculation per interface and the corresponding dashboard chart.

These new fields provide administrators with fine-grained control over the analytical output, ensuring that dashboards and reports reflect the most actionable and meaningful insights for migration planning.

Excel Report: Enhanced Full Evaluation Results and Eval by Integration Scenario

The Excel report has been enhanced with new columns in two key tabs to reflect the migration trend and tool coverage information at the rule and interface level.

Full Evaluation Results Tab

A new column "Migration Tool Coverage" (Yes/No) has been added to the Full Evaluation Results sheet. This column indicates, for each individual rule triggered for an interface, whether that rule's assessed capability is covered by SAP migration tooling.

This provides granular visibility into which specific technical characteristics of an interface can be addressed through automated migration tools.

Eval by Integration Scenario Tab

The Eval by Integration Scenario sheet now includes the following new columns, positioned after the Assessment Category column:

  • Migration Readiness (Ready to Migrate): The weighted percentage of the interface's rules that fall into the "Migrate" category.
  • Migration Readiness (Adjustment Required): The weighted percentage falling into the "Adapt" category.
  • Migration Readiness (Evaluation Required): The weighted percentage falling into the "Evaluate" category.
  • Migration Tool Coverage: A classification (Low, Medium, High, Very High) indicating the extent to which SAP migration tooling supports the interface, based on the percentage of rules with tool coverage.

The migration readiness percentages are calculated by summing the weights of all rules triggered for an interface, grouping them by assessment category, and computing the proportion each category represents of the total weight. The Migration Tool Coverage classification uses the following ranges: Low (up to 30%), Medium (up to 60%), High (up to 80%), and Very High (above 80%).

Additionally, the "Extraction Status" column has been repositioned to appear directly after the "Integration Scenario" column for improved readability.

PDF Report: Migration Analytics Overview

Conclusion

This enhancement transforms the Migration Assessment into a comprehensive analytical tool that provides transparency into the true distribution of migration effort across your integration landscape. By introducing migration readiness trends, tool coverage indicators, rule impact analysis, and effort concentration insights, the assessment now supports informed decision-making at both the technical and strategic level.

We recommend running a new assessment with the updated tool to take advantage of these capabilities. Review the new dashboard charts, explore the enhanced Excel columns, and use the PDF report's Migration Analytics Overview section to communicate findings to your stakeholders.

entry.title: Migrating Interface Split & Multiple Operation Using the Migration Tool in SAP Integration Suite
entry.content:
This blog post is part of the series Master Blog: SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite Migration – Tool and Guidance exploring how to migrate various integration patterns from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite using the Migration Tool. In this blog, we will explore the Interface Split and Multiple Operation. 

Objective of this Blog 

The goal of this blog is to explain how the Migration Tool supports the Interface Split and Multiple Operation Integration scenarios. The blog will cover the following key areas: 

Interface Split 

  • What is Interface Split in SAP Process Orchestration 
  • Migration of Interface Split by Standard Approach and Pipeline Approach 

Multiple Operation 

  • What is Multiple Operation in SAP Process Orchestration 
  • Not Operation-specific and Operation-specific 
  • Migration of Multiple Operation by Standard Approach 

 

Interface Split 

What is Interface Split in SAP Process Orchestration 

Interface Split in SAP Process Orchestration is a mechanism that routes a single incoming message from a sender system to multiple distinct receiver interfaces. Rather than handling multiple receiver interface scenarios within a single, complex integration flow, an Interface Split leverages Content Modifier, Script, and Router Steps in Cloud Integration to evaluate message payloads (JSON/XML fields, attributes, or headers) at runtime and dispatch the message to all receiver interfaces whose conditions are satisfied. This enables decoupled, parallel processing without requiring the sender system to split messages beforehand. 

 

Migration of Interface Split by Standard Approach and Pipeline Approach 

 

Interface Split scenario in the SAP Process Orchestration 

In this scenario, two conditions are defined for message splits that route to matching interfaces. The Receiver Determination contains one receiver only, with no receiver condition. Receiver Interface Conditions are inclusive, allowing multiple messages to be sent simultaneously. Each Receiver Interface can have its own operation mapping.

Migration Pattern & Approach

In Step 3 of the Migration Wizard — Choose Pattern and Approach — you select the appropriate migration pattern and the corresponding approach based on your integration scenario.   

Interface Split scenarios can be migrated using both the CBR (Content-Based Routing) Asynchronous and RL (Recipient List) Asynchronous patterns.

For this scenario, the RL Asynchronous pattern is recommended because it supports routing the message to multiple receivers simultaneously.

Standard Approach

For the Approach, both the Standard Approach and the Pipeline Approach are supported in SAP Integration Suite. First, let's go over the interface split scenario using the standard approach.

After a successful migration, a Summary Page is displayed, providing key insights and direct navigation links to the migrated artifacts in Cloud Integration.

Inbound Integration Process 

 

This process receives the message from the sender, sets the sender system and message type, and performs receiver determination along with receiver interface determination, where the defined receiver rules and routing conditions are evaluated.

When a receiver maintains multiple interfaces, specific Exchange Properties with an IFx suffix are generated. Since there are two Receiver Interfaces defined for Receiver_1 in this example, the generated properties are:

  • SAP-IFDET-RL_Receiver_1~IF1
  • SAP-IFDET-RL_Receiver_1~IF2

The interface split condition is evaluated at this point to identify the appropriate receiver based on the message content. These exchange properties collectively store the migrated receiver and interface rules, enabling the integration flow to evaluate routing logic dynamically at runtime.

For more details of exchange properties for the Receiver determination, see: Migrating Content-Based Routing Scenarios Using the Migration Tool in SAP Integration Suite

The Interface Determination and Merge XML Receivers steps are implemented as a Groovy script that evaluates predefined receiver and interface conditions. Based on these conditions, the script filters and identifies the valid interfaces for the current message, automatically validating them against the receiver list and operation type. It then merges the matching results into a single structured XML payload to enable dynamic message routing.

Outbound Integration

The Outbound Integration Process contains the mappings, receiver communication channels, and configured receivers. It is responsible for delivering the processed message to the final target system.

Router：

During the outbound phase, the routing logic utilizes the receiver interface information captured during inbound processing to link the appropriate interface mappings and communication channels to the specific recipient. Following the SAP_Interface header, the message is dynamically directed along the correct path to ensure accurate delivery to its destination.

Pipeline Approach

This section demonstrates the Pipeline Approach for migrating the same scenario. A pipeline represents the complete set of processing steps for a message. It consists of pipeline elements that call pipeline services — for example, carrying out mappings or routing messages to different receivers.

 

Key Highlights in the Migration Wizard

Once the Pipeline Approach is selected in Step 3, the Migration Tool enables you to adjust alternative partner details and verify or update the migrated receiver/interface conditions and endpoints, as shown below. 

After a successful migration, an overview of all generated artifacts is displayed.

The PID along with the associated parameters will be generated. In the Partner Directory tab you will have an overview. 

In the Binary Parameters tab, a specific parameter named receiverDetermination has been successfully created with an XSL content type. It will be used for determining the appropriate receivers. 

For more information, See Using the Partner Directory in the Pipeline Concept

 

Multiple Operation

What is Multiple Operation in SAP Process Orchestration

Multiple Operation in SAP Process Orchestration is a mechanism that allows a single message mapping to process multiple different sources and/or target operations (interfaces) within a single integration step.

Instead of creating separate, individual mapping objects for every single interface pair, a Multiple Operation scenario consolidates them. It enables the integration engine to bundle different message types or operations together, allowing to define complex 1:N (one-to-many), M:1 (many-to-one), or M:N (many-to-many) relationships between sender and receiver operations.

 

Operation-specific and Not Operation-specific

When configuring integration flows for a Multiple Operation service interface, these two modes determine how routing and processing rules are applied to the different operations within that single interface:

  • Operation-specific: This mode allows you to define unique receiver routing and mapping rules individually for each separate operation within the multiple operation interface. At runtime, the system evaluates which specific operation is active in the message payload and executes its dedicated processing path.
  • Not Operation-specific: This mode applies a single, unified routing and processing rule across all operations contained within the interface. Regardless of which specific operation the incoming message represents, the system handles it using the same global configuration without differentiating between them.

Operation-specific

This scenario has two different operations (Type1 and Type2), each with a specific condition per receiver — resulting in two conditions defined per operation. In this case, the condition is based on the value of the MANDT field of the incoming message, as shown in the screenshot below:

It is possible to check in the screenshot below that we need to use “operation-specific” option on Receiver tab to use multiple operations.

The Type1 Operation is defined with two different receivers with different operation mappings. As you can see below, for BC_PIMAS_Receiver, the Operation Mapping defined is OM_MaterialMultiOps_Op1_TC2_v2 

Integration Flow in Cloud Integration

Inbound Integration Process

The predefined conditions generated in the Content Modifier from the receiver determination and interface determination. SAP-OperationSpecific will be set up as TRUE in this case. 

The conditions will be assigned to the following exchange properties. SAP-DYNREC is a prefix added to each Receiver Communication Component present in the migrated ICO.

SAP-DYNREC-Type1~BC_PIMAS_Receiver

SAP-DYNREC-Type2~BC_PIMAS_Receiver

SAP-DYNREC-Type1~BC_PIMAS_Receiver_2

The Boolean true() will be defined for the following. SAP-IFDET is the prefix used for Interface Determination and is also added to the Receiver Communication Component name. The suffix ~IFx acts as an interface index indicator, which increments based on the number of receiver interfaces maintained for that receiver.

SAP-IFDET-Type2~BC_PIMAS_Receiver~IF1

SAP-IFDET-Type1~BC_PIMAS_Receiver~IF2

SAP-IFDET-Type1~BC_PIMAS_Receiver_2~IF1

 

Outbound Integration Process

These routers will evaluate the condition and then send the message to the correct operation mapping and subsequently send the message for the correct receiver.

The message is first routed to the correct operation via the following Router:

It is then routed to the correct receivers. 

 

The interface has multiple operations (Type1 and Type2) with two receiver systems. After identifying the operation type, the Integration Flow uses two different routers — one for each operation — to identify the correct receiver.

Not Operation-specific

This test case can be interpreted as Interface Split, as there are conditions on the Receiver Interface side. The "not operation-specific" option should be set to "true" on the receiver tab, indicating that one receiver handles incoming messages regardless of the operation type.

In this scenario, all data is sent to two receivers (BC_PIMAS_Receiver and BC_PIMAS_Receiver2) for the two different operations (Type1 and Type2), as shown below:

For BC_PIMAS_Receiver, each operation has three different operation mappings, each defined by a specific condition. These conditions apply rules depending on the incoming message, as shown below for Operation Type1 and Type2.

For BC_PIMAS_Receiver2, each operation has a single operation mapping with no conditions defined for both Operation Type1 and Type2, as shown below:

Integration Flow in Cloud Integration

Migration Wizard

Note: Only Standard Approach is supported for the multiple Operation Scenario.

While the Migration Tool does not currently provide automated generation of a Pipeline-based implementation for Multiple Operation scenarios, the migrated content can be adjusted manually to run within the Pipeline Approach. This mainly involves transferring the receiver/interface determination configuration to the Partner Directory, maintaining the corresponding pipeline parameters, and aligning the generated routing logic with the pipeline services. The required adjustments are typically limited and can be implemented without significant changes to the migrated integration logic. 

Inbound Integration Process

 

The predefined conditions generated in the Content Modifier from the receiver determination and interface determination. No Value has been set up for the SAP-OperationSpecific in this case. It will be used in the next step Interface Determination Script to get the OperationSpecfic dynamically.

Outbound Integration Process

It sends the message to the right receiver first and then route it to the correct operation.

 

Post-Migration Activities – Key Points to Keep in Mind:

After successfully migrating Interface Split and Multiple Operation scenarios into an Integration Flow, the following activities should be verified and completed:

  1. Verify Migrated Artifacts: Ensure that mappings (local and global), Function Libraries, imported archives, and Local UDFs are migrated correctly and functioning as expected.
  2. Adapter Configuration: Adapter parameters are externalized. Verify the configurations and update them as needed to match the target environment.
  3. Adapter Conversions: Adapter conversions such as JSON-to-XML or CSV-to-XML are migrated automatically. Check the configuration in the conversion flow steps and adjust if necessary.
  4. Security Artifacts: The Migration Tool does not create or import security artifacts in Cloud Integration. Manual creation of security materials (certificates, keystores, etc.) is a prerequisite before deploying the Integration Flow.
  5. Reusable Mapping Options: If the “Enable Reusable Mapping” option was selected during migration, ensure that the standalone artifacts are deployed first before deploying the main Integration Flow.

entry.title: Automation of Communication Channel Monitoring in SAP PI/PO
entry.content:
In one of my SAP PI/PO landscapes, we had a requirement to monitor the health and availability of communication channels without manually logging into NWA or Communication Channel Monitoring. The operations team needed a lightweight mechanism to retrieve channel status information, activation state, and error details that could be consumed by external monitoring tools and dashboards.

To address this requirement, I designed an interface that leverages the Adapter Framework Channel Administration service to retrieve communication channel information in real time. The solution automatically collects channel details, formats the response into a consumable XML structure, and makes it available for monitoring and reporting purposes. This significantly reduced manual monitoring effort and provided a centralized view of communication channel health across the PI/PO landscape.

Using the Adapter Framework service, SAP PI/PO provides channel status information through an XML response. By leveraging the provided XSD and creating request/response mappings, you can build an interface that retrieves:

  • Complete list of communication channels
  • Channel status and activation state
  • Adapter type and direction
  • Error details and short logs
  • Control information

    The response can then be consumed by external monitoring applications, dashboards, or reporting solutions.

    Adapter Framework XSD

    SAP provides the response structure through the following URL:

    https://<host>:<port>/AdapterFramework/channelAdmin/ChannelAdmin.xsd

    Step 1: Create Request Data Type

    Create a simple request Data Type with a single string field.

    The request payload only requires a string value to trigger the channel status retrieval.

    Request Structure:


    Step 2: Create Request Mapping

    Create a Message Type based on Data type and perform a simple request mapping.

    Since only a string input is required, map the source string directly to the target structure.

    Request Mapping:

    Step 3: Import Response XSD

    Import the XSD downloaded from: https://<host>:<port>/AdapterFramework/channelAdmin/ChannelAdmin.xsd

    The response message structure contains detailed channel information.

    Step 4: Create Response Mapping

    Create a response message type based on the imported XSD and map the required fields from the Adapter Framework response to your custom response structure.

    Typical fields to expose include:

    • Service
    • Channel Name
    • Adapter Type
    • Direction
    • Activation State
    • Error Log

    This ensures the monitoring interface returns a clean and consumable XML response.

    Step 5: Add XSLT Mapping

    After the response mapping, add the following XSLT mapping to format the output and make it easier to consume by monitoring tools or dashboards.


    Step 6: Configure Of IB

    In this scenario:

    • Sender Adapter: SFTP
    • Receiver Adapter: REST

    The SFTP sender is used to trigger the process, while the REST receiver invokes the SAP PI/PO Channel Administration service and retrieves the communication channel details.

    Sender Configuration:

    Configure an SFTP Sender Channel that places a trigger file (or request payload) into the SFTP location.

    The monitoring process is initiated by dropping an empty file into the configured SFTP directory. The file acts only as a scheduler/trigger and does not contain any payload.

    SFTP sender channel is configured to poll a specific directory.

    Whenever an empty file is placed in the source location, SAP PI/PO picks up the file and triggers the integration flow.

    Request Response Bean Configuration

    Since the integration is initiated by an empty file through the SFTP Sender Channel, the sender channel must be configured with the RequestResponseBean module. This allows SAP PI/PO to operate in a synchronous manner and capture the response returned by the REST receiver endpoint.

    Without the RequestResponseBean, the SFTP sender would simply trigger the interface and complete processing without receiving the channel status response from the Channel Administration API.

    Sender Channel Module Configuration

    Configure the following module in the SFTP Sender Communication Channel:

    Why RequestResponseBean is Required?

    The RequestResponseBean:

    • Converts the processing from asynchronous to synchronous.
    • Waits for the response from the receiver endpoint.
    • Captures the response payload returned by the REST API.
    • Makes the response available for subsequent response mapping and XSLT processing.
    • Enables retrieval of communication channel status data within the same integration flow.

    Step 7: Configure the REST Receiver Communication Channel

    The Receiver Communication Channel is configured using the REST Adapter to invoke the SAP PI/PO Adapter Framework Channel Administration API.

    Endpoint URL

    Configure the REST receiver with the following URL: https://<host>:<port>/AdapterFramework/ChannelAdminServlet?party=*&service=*&channel=*&action=status

    HTTP Operation: GET
    Response Format: XML

    End-to-End Processing

    Once an empty file is dropped into the SFTP source directory:

    1. SFTP Sender Channel picks up the file.
    2. RequestResponseBean enables synchronous processing.
    3. Request Mapping generates the required request payload.
    4. REST Receiver Channel invokes: ChannelAdminServlet
    5. Channel Administration Servlet retrieves all channel statuses.
    6. XML response is returned to PI/PO.
    7. Response Mapping extracts the required fields.
    8. XSLT Mapping formats the final report.
    9. The final output contains a consolidated communication channel monitoring report.
       

    Why Use ChannelAdminServlet?

    TheChannelAdminServlet provides a lightweight and efficient way to obtain runtime channel information without navigating through NWA manually.

    Benefits

    • Retrieves all communication channels in a single call.
    • Provides real-time activation status.
    • Displays channel error messages through ShortLog.
    • Supports monitoring of Sender and Receiver channels.
    • Can be integrated with external monitoring tools and dashboards.
    • Enables automated health-check reporting through PI/PO interfaces
    This design enables a fully automated Communication Channel Monitoring solution in SAP PI/PO, where an empty SFTP trigger file initiates a synchronous process and the REST Receiver Adapter calls the ChannelAdminServlet API to retrieve the status and error details of all communication channels in the landscape.

    Hope you enjoyed the blog!!!!
    Happy Integrating!!!
    Sai Prudhvi Raj Taduva
    SAP PI/PO & SAP Integration Specialist 🚀

entry.title: How to Generate a WSDL / SOAP API in SAP PO 7.5 Single Stack

Introduction: In this blog, I will explain how to generate and expose a WSDL/SOAP API in SAP Process Orchestration (SAP PO) 7.5 Single Stack and how it can be consumed as part of an integration scenario.

The integration scenario covered in this blog is:

                                           Azure → SAP PO → SAP S/4HANA

The objective is to expose a SOAP-based API from SAP PO, generate the corresponding WSDL, and make the service available for consumption from Azure.

The complete process can be divided into two major areas:

  1. Enterprise Services Repository (ESR) – where the required design-time objects are created.
  2. Integration Directory (ID) – where the integration configuration and SOAP service exposure are configured.

Prerequisite: Before configuring the SOAP API in the Integration Directory, the required ESR objects should be completed.

The ESR development typically includes the required:

  • Data Types
  • Message Types
  • Service Interfaces
  • Other required design-time objects

Once the ESR development is completed and activated, we can proceed with the corresponding configuration in the Integration Directory (ID).

End-to-End Integration Flow:

The high-level flow used in this scenario is:

Azure → SOAP API → SAP PO → S/4HANA

Azure acts as the source system and sends the SOAP request to the SOAP endpoint exposed by SAP PO.SAP PO receives the request, processes it according to the configured integration scenario, and then sends the required message to SAP S/4HANA.

The WSDL generated/exposed through the SAP PO configuration provides the contract that the consuming application can use to understand the SOAP service, including the available operations and message structures.

ESR Development:
The first step is to complete the required interface development in the Enterprise Services Repository (ESR).

The required objects should be created according to the integration requirement. Once the ESR development is completed, the objects should be activated and made available for the Integration Directory configuration.

It is important to complete the ESR development before proceeding with the corresponding Integration Directory configuration because the ID configuration uses the interfaces and other objects defined in ESR.

Integration Directory Configuration:
After completing the ESR development, we can move to the Integration Directory (ID).
Here, we configure the integration scenario and the required communication channels.

For the SOAP API exposure, the relevant SOAP configuration is maintained on the sender side. Based on this configuration, SAP PO can expose the required SOAP endpoint and provide the corresponding WSDL information.

The detailed configuration steps, including how to generate/access the WSDL and configure the SOAP endpoint, will be covered step by step in the following sections.

STEPS:
Below is the Channel Created for SOAP Sender since the Scenario is Asynchronous, we are using the quality of service as Exactly once.

After Creating the Sender Channel, we are proceeding with the creation of Integrated Configuration. We are selecting the Service Interface created in ESR while creating the ICO.

After Creating the ICO we are assigning the sender and receiver channels and using Operation mapping which is created in ESR and activate the ICO.

 Now right click on the Integration Configuration and select Display WSDL option


Below WSDL screen will appear and we will save the WSDL. 

We are using the SOAP UI for Providing the API. Click on the SOAP tile and then upload the saved WSDL through browse.

 

After clicking on the Ok then the WSDL is loaded and expand the section
 

 

After selecting the request, we will get endpoint

 

 Depending on the environment and security requirements, the service may be accessed through HTTP or HTTPS.


Once the SOAP service is configured, the endpoint can be tested with necessary credentials so that we can know it is hitting our SAP PO system. In below we have successfully sent the request to the SAP PO system.

In SAP PO we have successfully received the request and delivered to the SAP PO.We can see the same request which was sent from SOAP UI and SAP PO has received the request and processed the same to S4 Hana.

 

Now we can conclude that the endpoint is valid and we can share the same endpoint to Source (Azure) with necessary credentials so that they can establish the connection with SAP PO.

For production integrations, HTTPS is generally preferred because it provides encryption for the communication between the consumer and the SAP PO endpoint.

Note: 
Since the required connectivity between the internal Azure environment and SAP PO is already established and the network/firewall rules permit the required traffic, no additional IP whitelisting is required for this integration.

Conclusion:

entry.title: What SAP Process Integration/Process Orchestration Customers Need to Know About the 2030 Timeline
entry.content:
SAP recently published guidance covering the implications of the 2030 maintenance timeline for SAP Business Suite 7 and SAP NetWeaver customers. If you are running SAP Process Orchestration (PO) or SAP Process Integration (PI) — even if you have already moved off SAP ERP or SAP Business Suite 7 — this article is relevant to you.

Why This Matters for PI/PO Customers

SAP Process Orchestration and SAP Process Integration are built on SAP NetWeaver Application Server 7.5 for Java (NW AS Java). As outlined in the guidance, SAP's current support arrangements for Java used with NW AS Java 7.5 are scheduled to conclude at the end of 2030. This constraint applies to PI/PO independently of whether you are also running SAP Business Suite 7.

To state this precisely:

  • Mainstream maintenance for SAP Process Orchestration 7.5: ends December 31, 2027
  • Optional extended maintenance: runs through December 31, 2030
  • After 2030: customer-specific maintenance (CSM) — without a follow-on release.
  • For SAP Process Orchestration, Private Cloud Edition (PO PCE): maintenance ends December 31, 2030. Refer to SAP Note 3833114.

Entering customer-specific maintenance (CSM) without a follow-on release goes beyond a standard end-of-maintenance message. At the end of 2030, SAP's support arrangements for Java used with NW AS Java 7.5 shall expire,. After this point, SAP will not be able to provide comprehensive support for Java or database-related issues in these environments. This makes CSM an unsustainable long-term model for business-critical integration infrastructure.

The Path Forward

SAP Integration Suite is SAP's strategic integration platform, trusted by enterprises worldwide to support all integration patterns while enabling customers to scale, secure, and govern their holistic integration landscape. SAP has invested extensively to help ensure SAP Integration Suite supports all current integration patterns while future-proofing your integration landscape — delivering AI-ready capabilities that enable you to connect AI agents, create intelligent processes that are reliable, secure and can scale, and govern your modern enterprise-wide digital ecosystem with confidence.

Key capabilities include:

  • 250+ prebuilt adapters (most of them to integrate with 3rdP), and 5,100+ prebuilt integration content packages for fast time-to-value
  • Edge Integration Cell for hybrid and on-premise-connected scenarios
  • Foundation for AI enablement-  MCP Gateway, governance and security for AI agents (Ref: Agentic AI & AI Agents | SAP Architecture Center)
  • AI-enabled development and operations features
  • Modern integration patterns : API management, Trading Partner Management, (Advanced) Event Mesh, MCP/AI gateway and an LLM adapter to integrate with agents and LLMs
  • Automated assessments and AI-supported migration tooling for PO/PI landscapes
  • Extensive transition expertise available across all regions via our partner ecosystem.

 

Whether your focus is on connecting hybrid landscapes, accelerating AI-driven automation, enabling API and event-driven architectures, connecting with business partners through industry-specific B2B standards, or aligning with a clean core approach, consider SAP Integration Suite is designed to support all these needs. We have made it our mission to make your transition with minimal disruption and maximal value for your future landscapes

What to Do Next

entry.title: How to See Content of a TPZ File?
entry.content:
As more organizations move from SAP PI/PO toward SAP Integration Suite, one of the first challenges during migration is understanding what already exists in the legacy integration landscape.

In an ideal scenario, we still have access to the original SAP PI/PO development system and can inspect the Enterprise Services Repository directly.

In practice, this is not always the case.

Sometimes we only have exported TPZ files. In other situations, we need to analyze a large number of historical mappings without continuously navigating through the original PI/PO system.

This was the motivation behind a small project I started for my own analysis work:

Open Tpz Master

Open Tpz Master is an open-source desktop application designed to analyze SAP PI/PO TPZ exports and make their Message Mapping structures easier to understand outside the original SAP environment.

The Problem

A TPZ export can contain valuable information about PI/PO design-time objects.

However, having the TPZ file is very different from having a convenient way to understand its contents.

This becomes particularly noticeable with Message Mappings.

A mapping may contain:

  • source and target fields

  • standard mapping functions

  • constants

  • nested functions

  • conditions

  • context operations

  • user-defined functions

  • Java code

  • multiple levels of function arguments

When analyzing an unfamiliar interface, understanding these relationships manually can take significant time.

The problem becomes even more relevant during PI/PO to Integration Suite migrations.

Before rebuilding an integration, we normally need to answer questions such as:

  • What does this mapping actually do?

  • Which source fields are used?

  • Which functions are applied?

  • Are User Defined Functions involved?

  • How complex is the mapping?

  • Which schemas are used?

  • Which parts can be migrated directly?

  • Which parts may require redesign?

This led me to experiment with parsing the exported mapping artifacts directly.

Introducing Open Tpz Master

Open Tpz Master reads a TPZ export and extracts supported Message Mapping information from it.

The basic workflow is:

TPZ Export
    |
    v
Extract Mapping Artifacts
    |
    v
Parse Mapping Metadata
    |
    v
Discover Mapping Bricks
    |
    v
Build Mapping Tree
    |
    v
Visualize Mapping Logic

The important point is that this analysis happens locally.

The tool does not require a connection to the original SAP PI/PO system.

Discovering Message Mappings

After loading a TPZ file, Open Tpz Master searches the exported content for supported Message Mapping artifacts.

Detected mappings are displayed in the application.

The user can select an individual mapping and inspect the metadata extracted from the TPZ.

This is useful when a TPZ contains multiple mappings because the archive can be explored without manually navigating through its internal XML structures.

Visualizing Mapping Logic

The part I found most useful during development was converting the mapping definition into a visual structure.

Instead of displaying only the raw mapping XML, Open Tpz Master builds a top-down brick tree representing the mapping logic.

A simplified example could look like this:

Target
  |
  if
  |
  +-------------------+
  |         |         |
  |         |         |
  UDF    stringEquals Source
            |
       +----+----+
       |         |
      trim      const
       |
  mapWithDefault
       |
     Source

Each node represents a mapping brick.

Depending on the mapping, a brick may represent:

  • Source

  • Target

  • Function

  • Constant

  • User Defined Function

  • Mapping operation

The tree makes the relationship between nested mapping functions much easier to inspect.

This is especially helpful when several functions are nested inside one another.

Inspecting Mapping Bricks

Selecting a brick in the graph displays additional information about it.

For example, for a function the tool can expose information such as:

Name:     readRefreshToken
Type:     udf
Category: function
UUID:     brick_5

Function arguments and other available metadata can also be inspected.

This allows the graph to remain relatively simple while detailed technical information is available when required.

User Defined Functions

User Defined Functions are particularly interesting during migration analysis.

Standard graphical mapping functions are usually relatively straightforward to understand.

A UDF can contain arbitrary Java logic.

For this reason, simply knowing that a UDF exists is often not enough.

Open Tpz Master can identify supported UDF definitions and display the associated Java implementation when it is available in the exported mapping metadata.

For example, selecting a UDF node can expose the corresponding implementation in a separate details panel.

This can help answer an important migration question:

Is this mapping purely graphical, or does it contain custom Java logic that needs additional analysis?

Raw Metadata

During development I intentionally kept access to the underlying metadata available.

Although the visual representation is more convenient for normal analysis, sometimes it is necessary to understand exactly how a particular mapping element is represented in the TPZ export.

For this reason, the application can also expose the relevant raw XML metadata.

This has also been useful while improving the parser itself.

 

Why Offline Analysis?

One design decision was important to me from the beginning:

TPZ analysis should be possible completely locally.

Integration artifacts may contain information about customer landscapes, interface structures and custom business logic.

For consultants working with customer systems, uploading these artifacts to an external analysis service may not always be acceptable.

Open Tpz Master therefore performs the analysis on the local machine.

No SAP system connection is required for the core TPZ analysis.

Why Open Source?

The first version of Open Tpz Master is being developed as an open-source Community Edition.

There are several reasons for this.

First, TPZ files come from many different PI/PO systems and releases. Real-world mappings are much more diverse than the examples available during development.

Community feedback can therefore help identify:

  • unsupported mapping structures,

  • unusual function combinations,

  • parsing problems,

  • visualization problems,

  • differences between PI/PO versions.

Second, integration artifacts can contain sensitive information.

For a local analysis tool, being able to inspect the source code can provide additional transparency about how files are processed.

Finally, I would like the initial version to be useful by itself rather than simply being a demonstration.

Current Scope

The initial Community Edition focuses primarily on:

  • TPZ file analysis

  • Message Mapping discovery

  • Message Mapping metadata extraction

  • graphical mapping analysis

  • top-down brick-tree visualization

  • standard mapping function inspection

  • User Defined Function inspection

  • Java UDF code inspection where available

  • raw mapping metadata inspection

  • XSD extraction

  • local/offline processing

The project is still under development, so compatibility with every possible PI/PO mapping structure should not yet be assumed.

Where This Could Go Next

There are several directions I am currently investigating.

One obvious area is improving Message Mapping analysis itself.

Other potential areas include:

  • Mapping comparison

  • Function Library analysis

  • Java Mapping analysis

  • XSLT analysis

  • Communication Channel analysis

  • cross-object dependency analysis

  • where-used analysis

  • complexity scoring

  • automated technical documentation

  • PI/PO to Integration Suite migration assessment

However, I do not want to build these features based only on assumptions.

One of the reasons for publishing the project is to understand which capabilities SAP integration consultants actually find useful.

A Bigger Goal: Migration Analysis

Longer term, I think TPZ analysis can be useful beyond simply displaying Message Mappings.

Consider a migration assessment where an analyzer could identify something like:

Interface
│
├── Message Mapping
│   ├── 37 field mappings
│   ├── 12 standard functions
│   ├── 3 UDFs
│   └── 1 Function Library dependency
│
├── Communication Channel
│   └── SOAP
│
└── Migration Assessment
    ├── Standard mapping: compatible
    ├── UDF: review required
    ├── Java dependency: detected
    └── Estimated complexity: Medium

This is not the current scope of the Community Edition, but it represents an interesting direction for future development.

Instead of simply asking:

"What objects exist in this TPZ?"

we could eventually ask:

"What will I need to consider when migrating these objects?"

That is where I believe this type of tooling could become particularly useful for PI/PO migration projects.

Feedback from the SAP Integration Community

The project is still evolving, and feedback from people working with real SAP PI/PO landscapes would be extremely valuable.

I am particularly interested in hearing about:

  • mapping structures that are difficult to analyze,

  • TPZ files that behave differently from expected,

  • functions that are not represented correctly,

  • information you normally need during migration analysis,

  • features that would save time during PI/PO projects.

Bug reports and feature requests will be managed through GitLab Issues.

When sharing examples publicly, please make sure that TPZ files, XML, screenshots and schemas do not contain confidential customer information.

Sanitized or synthetic examples are preferable.

Conclusion

Open Tpz Master started from a relatively simple requirement:

I have a TPZ file. How can I understand the Message Mapping without having the original PI/PO system available?

That gradually turned into parsing mapping structures, reconstructing function relationships, visualizing them as trees, inspecting UDFs and extracting schemas.

There is still a lot that can be improved.

But I believe TPZ exports contain enough information to make offline analysis useful, particularly as more PI/PO landscapes move toward SAP Integration Suite.

I am publishing the Community Edition to see whether other SAP integration consultants encounter the same problems and, more importantly, what they would expect from such a tool.

Feedback and contributions are welcome.
